Tensor products and parameter-dependent distributions

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, September 2026. Self-checked by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort. Public domain (CC0).

Source/proof self-check and prerequisite integration by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. Historical authorship and component terms are retained.

Two independent singular measurements should combine into a measurement on a product space. Knowing its value on separated tests is only the beginning: a general test function need not be a product. This lesson constructs the combined distribution, proves that the order of the two pairings does not matter, and identifies its support exactly. Parameter-dependent pairings also explain a support condition that cannot be omitted.

The preceding kernel lesson supplies the topology of test spaces, bounded test families, support localization and density of products in both the test and Schwartz spaces. The smoothing lesson supplies compact distributions, uniform-boundedness estimates and the complete integral Taylor proof, including derivative seminorms and signed increments. The supplied scalar calculus foundation, §§12–13, proves the compactness, finite-coordinate calculus and cutoff inputs; the functional foundation, §§6, 14.1–14.2 and 19, proves Baire's theorem and completeness in the exact smooth seminorms. The measure foundation, §§15.0–15.1, supplies integration and Fubini. The pairing is bilinear. Exact external comparisons and related kernel references are listed at the end; the programme proofs used here are supplied through these preceding lessons and components.

Pairing with a moving smooth test

Let , be open, and let . Suppose has the following local uniform-support property: for every compact parameter set , there is such that for in a neighborhood of and .

Lemma 1.1 (parameter differentiation). Under these hypotheses, is smooth, and If is compactly supported, the uniform-support hypothesis on is unnecessary.

Proof. On a compact parameter neighborhood, use a common support and a distribution estimate . A difference quotient of in a parameter coordinate converges to the corresponding derivative in the seminorm in , uniformly on smaller compact parameter sets. Taylor's formula gives this explicitly: the remainder, including every -derivative through order , is bounded by a constant times the parameter increment, using mixed derivatives on the compact product. Pairing transfers that convergence to the scalar difference quotient of . Repeating the argument proves all derivatives and their continuity. For compact , choose a fixed cutoff equal to one near its support and replace by that cutoff times . This supplies the uniform support and leaves every pairing unchanged.

The support requirement is local in the parameter, rather than a single support condition for all of . It prevents a test family from transporting unbounded information into the pairing from infinity.

Reversing the variables gives another distribution with the same property. Product tests are dense by Lemma 3.1 of the kernel lesson, so the two distributions agree and the product is unique.

If an output point is outside , one of its coordinates has a neighborhood where the corresponding factor vanishes. Formula (2.2), with that factor paired last, shows that the product distribution vanishes on a product neighborhood. This proves the inclusion in (2.3).

Conversely, let , . Every product neighborhood of contains tests , with , ; otherwise one factor would vanish on that neighborhood. Their product pairing is nonzero. Thus belongs to the product support. If either factor is zero, both sides of (2.3) are empty, so that case is included.

For compact factors, use separate cutoffs equal to one near their supports. Applying the preceding construction to the cut-off defines the product on all smooth functions. Lemma 1.1 for compact distributions makes both inner pairings smooth without support restrictions. The outer factors see only the region where the cutoffs equal one, so both formulas remain valid and independent of the cutoffs.

Estimate (2.4) gives order at most on the compact product. It does not assert equality of orders for arbitrary distributions.

For a smooth multiplier , the definition is . It gives a distribution: multiplication preserves the support of , and the finite Leibniz formula bounds every derivative of through order on a compact by a constant, depending on the derivatives of on , times . The test-space mapping property in the kernel lesson then gives continuity. Distributional derivatives are defined by ; the same argument, with , gives their continuity.

Corollary 2.2 (derivatives, separated multipliers and three factors). For smooth on , on , Tensor products of three factors are associative after the natural identification of the product spaces. Interchanging two factors interchanges the corresponding variables.

Proof. Apply the definitions of distributional derivative and smooth multiplication to a product test. The signs in differentiating its two factors multiply to , exactly the sign of the derivative on the whole product. Each side of every identity is a distribution and agrees on all product tests, so uniqueness proves the identities. For three factors, both associations give on threefold products. Such products are dense by the same cut-off periodic expansion used for two factors, now in three groups of variables. Uniqueness again proves the assertion.

Tempered products

Theorem 4.1. If , , their tensor product is tempered on . Both formulas (2.2) are valid for every Schwartz function , and define the same product as the local distribution construction.

Proof. Use the Schwartz seminorms from the kernel lesson. Suppose . First justify differentiation without a compact support assumption. Every slice is Schwartz. For a nonzero real coordinate increment , the integral Taylor formula from the preceding lesson, applied also after every -derivative through order , gives Indeed the remainder is ; its -weight is bounded by the full product-space weight and its total derivative order is at most . The bound is uniform in . The first integral segment formula similarly bounds the -difference between the two slices by . Moving coordinates one at a time proves continuity for arbitrary parameter increments. Applying to these estimates proves, inductively, that are smooth, with all stated derivatives continuous.

Now the product weights give In detail, a derivative through order in , a derivative through order in , and the weight are controlled by the order seminorm on the whole product: each factor of the weight is bounded by the corresponding power of , and the total derivative order is at most . Thus is Schwartz and depends continuously on . Pairing it with , controlled by some , gives a fixed bound by .

Reversing the two pairings gives another tempered distribution agreeing on Schwartz product tests. Their density was proved by the spatial and frequency expansion in Lemma 5.1 of the kernel lesson. The two distributions agree. On compactly supported tests the formula is the local construction, so their restrictions agree as well.

Let have integral one, and define This is smooth on . Near any point , it is identically zero for sufficiently small positive , because its support escapes to infinity. Away from , ordinary composition is smooth. Every individual -test has compact support.

Nevertheless, for the distribution , which is discontinuous. Thus joint smoothness of and compact support of each individual test do not replace the local uniform-support hypothesis of Lemma 1.1. A compact distribution would only see a fixed bounded region in , so its paired value would eventually be zero near .

Solution 1. Since , The support is by Theorem 2.1. The derivative formula gives order at most one. It is not order zero: localize to a small neighborhood of either support point and choose a test of the form , with nonzero at that point and . The supremum of the test tends to zero while its pairing stays nonzero. Hence no order-zero estimate can hold.

Solution 2. We first justify the scalar regularity test being used. If a continuous complex-valued function induces the zero distribution on an open set, it vanishes pointwise. Otherwise, multiply it by a constant of modulus one so that its real part is positive at a chosen nonzero point. Continuity makes that real part positive on a ball; integration against a nonzero nonnegative smooth cutoff in that ball is then nonzero, a contradiction. Consequently continuous distributional representatives are unique. Local smooth representatives agree on overlaps by this argument and fit together to a smooth function on their union. The local distributional equalities hold on the union by the support localization and partition argument from the kernel lesson. Hence a largest open smooth locus exists and its complement is closed.

On the negative and positive half-lines the Heaviside distribution equals the ordinary functions zero and one, respectively. A smooth representative across zero would therefore have these pointwise values, contradicting continuity. The principal value equals on each open set away from zero by its defining integral in the kernel lesson. A smooth representative across zero would equal pointwise on the punctured neighborhood, again contradicting continuity. The scalar supports are and : on each indicated open half-line their nonzero values can be detected by small cutoffs, and the endpoints belong to the closed supports.

The support is . On , the distribution is zero; on , , it is the smooth function . Thus its singular support is contained in At with , the function is smooth and nonzero nearby. Pairing in with a small test of nonzero integral against leaves a nonzero multiple of the Heaviside distribution, which is not smooth at zero. If the two-variable distribution were smooth nearby, that localized pairing would be smooth, a contradiction.

At with , pairing in with a nonzero-integral test leaves a nonzero multiple of , which is not smooth at zero. Its failure to be smooth follows also from its ordinary value on the punctured line, which has no continuous extension. Finally is in the closure of these singular points, and singular support is closed. The stated containment is therefore equality.
